newsitem.title: USA: ABC's lineup overshadowed by executive drama.
newsitem.headline: ABC's lineup overshadowed by executive drama.

text.p: No. 3 network ABC rolled out its new fall lineup Monday to television critics, but found its on-air programming was no match for a different drama being played out in its own executive offices.
The big question was not how the network planned to lure viewers away from NBC's popular "Seinfeld," or if it had any new shows that might match the appeal of its own "N.Y.P.D. Blue."
What everyone was asking, instead, was whether Jamie Tarses, the embattled president of ABC Entertainment, would keep her job.

ABC tried to quell the speculation at the start of its three-day press tour by saying Tarses would be present, on Wednesday, to host an executive session along with Stuart Bloomberg, who was recently brought in as chairman of the entertainment division to oversee Tarses.

Still, the meeting continued to buzz with questions over how ABC would handle the embarassing publicity surrounding the 33-year-old Tarses, who made headlines a year ago when ABC hired her away from NBC, but has been criticised for not being up to turning around the network's flagging performance.
The buzz became louder two weeks ago when she was featured in a New York Times Magazine cover story, complaining of sexism and criticising her bosses at ABC and its parent, Walt Disney Co.

An ABC spokeswoman tried to make light of the matter at the start of the press tour, joking, "We've discovered that more journalists look forward to ABC's press tour than any other network's press tour."

In fact, the stir surrounding Tarses has been big enough to reach the NBC and CBS press tours, held last week. On Saturday, Warren Littlefield president for entertainment at NBC and Tarses' former boss there, offered words of sympathy.

"I absolutely do feel for her," Littlefield told reporters. "I can remember myself being in the crossfire of controversy, but I've never seen it like this. Do I think it's more difficult for a woman to be in the top levels of business than a man? Yeah, I do."

But as ABC got down to business Monday, it had at least one of Tarses' projects clearly on display: a new, risky ad campaign that is meant to win viewers by embracing rather than fighting the concept of TV as the "boob tube."

ABC hired Tarses because of her success at NBC developing hits like "Friends" and "Mad About You" that attracted the young, affluent, urban viewers advertisers pay top dollar for. When she joined ABC, Tarses hired a new ad agency in a bid to find a slogan to rival NBC'S catchy "Must See TV" campaign.

The result is a new slogan, "Television is Good," and a series of ads with tongue-in-cheek messages such as: "TV. What would you watch without it?" Some of the other ads in the $40 million campaign go further, with lines like "It's a Beautiful Day, What Are You Doing Outside?"; "The Couch is Your Friend"; "Don't Worry, You've Got Billions of Brain Cells," and "Life is Short. Watch TV."

"Our research showed that people tend to enjoy television a lot more than they say they do," said Alan Cohen, ABC's executive vice president for marketing. "We decided to play off of that and poke fun at the fact it's OK to watch TV."

Of course, delivering popular shows between the commercials is still the real challenge. As the network screens its new programmes in coming days, it will get a better sense of how well Tarses has succeeded with those who count the most -- the audiences.
Rival network NBC is owned by General Electric Co.
